newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Americas defense chiefs seek to avoid arms race.
newsitem.headline: Americas defense chiefs seek to avoid arms race.

text.p: Western hemisphere defence chiefs were meeting on Sunday for talks likely to focus on how to modernise Latin America's armed forces without setting off a regional arms race.

Defence ministers from the United States, Canada and 32 Latin American and Caribbean nations, with communist Cuba the only absentee, were looking at how to consolidate the subordination to civilian rule of armed forces that in many cases are just getting used to democracy.
But the issue which had some governments expressing most concern was U.S. sales of military hardware in the region.

In recognition of democratic reforms, Washington was considering scrapping a ban on sales of high-technology lethal weaponry to Latin America -- a policy change favoured by the Defence Department but looked on more warily by the State Department.

"We are very appreciative of the change that has occurred in the region, the fact that we now deal, with one exception, with democratic governments. But governments continue to have legitimate defence needs," said a senior U.S. defence official, who asked not to be named.

"We don't have any interest in seeing arms races in the hemisphere or any tensions arise out of legitimate arms modernisation processes which will inevitably occur," he added. "We see no reason why we should exclude ourselves from this process and we think it would be healthy for us to be involved."

But the possibility of their neighbours buying advanced weapons from the United States made some Latin American governments jumpy, especially those for whom violent border disputes were still a reality or a recent memory.

Peru and Ecuador fought a bloody jungle border war only last year, Venezuela and Colombia and Central American neighbours like Honduras and El Salvador continued to have tension on their borders, and Argentina nearly went to war with Chile in 1978.

Argentine Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez, hosting the talks in the Argentine Andean resort of Bariloche which follow a first defence summit last year, said he hoped it would encourage "dialogue and cooperation to avoid an arms race."
"The idea is for each country to know what resources other countries are spending on defence, and to maintain that at current levels."
Some Argentine defence officials, whose own budget has shrunk rapidly under the government of President Carlos Menem, are particularly concerned about Chile's interest in buying U.S. F-16 fighters.

Argentine Navy chief Admiral Jose Molina Pico ruffled feathers this week by saying that his country's military was so short of cash that if Chilean troops threatened the mountainous border, his country could not respond.
Dominguez told foreign correspondents this week: "What Chile wants is to maintain its operational level without increasing its offensive capacity, so we see no threat of conflict."

But in a visit to Washington last month the minister said that Chile buying advanced fighters "means introducing excessively sophisticated weaponry to the region at a time when it is neither convenient nor necessary."

Argentina, interested in buying U.S. helicopters, transport plans and munitions, signed an agreement with Brazil last month not to increase their military budgets -- citing the wish to avoid an arms escalation.
